highlights.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # E2E Networks to add 5.4 MW NVIDIA Blackwell AI capacity E2E Networks plans to add 5.4 MW of NVIDIA Blackwell GPU capacity, increasing its total AI infrastructure to 14.6 MW. This expansion aims to meet rising demand for AI computing in India, supporting various AI workloads. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 28, 2026 at 07:45 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * E2E Networks will add 5.4 MW of NVIDIA Blackwell GPU capacity, reaching 14.6 MW total. * The expansion targets rising demand from Indian AI startups, enterprises, and public-sector organisations. * A ₹1,000 crore deal with an Indian sovereign AI company secures Blackwell GPUs until June 2029. * Revenue for Q3 2026 increased 411 per cent year-on-year to ₹223.76 crore. Indian cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure provider [E2E Networks](/tag/e2e+networks) will add 5.4 megawatts (MW) of computing capacity powered by [NVIDIA Blackwell](/tag/nvidia+blackwell) GPUs, the company said on Tuesday. This expansion will increase its total AI factory capacity to approximately 14.6 MW, a nearly 59 per cent rise. The proposed infrastructure will include NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and other Blackwell graphics processing units (GPUs). The additional capacity is intended to support AI workloads ranging from foundation model training to production inference and multimodal applications. E2E Networks reported growing demand from AI startups, model developers, research institutions, enterprises, and public-sector organisations. Organisations handling sensitive data are seeking computing infrastructure hosted in [India](/tag/india). Tarun Dua, founder and managing director of E2E Networks, noted that India’s AI builders are consuming AI tokens at previously un-heard scales in production. Dua added that the company is expanding capacity to allow organisations to keep their data within their own boundaries under national laws. This announcement follows previous investments and customer commitments. In August, E2E Networks signed a binding term sheet worth approximately ₹1,000 crore, excluding taxes. This agreement is with an unnamed Indian [sovereign AI](/tag/sovereign+ai) company for NVIDIA Blackwell cloud GPUs and related services through June 2029. The agreement converts deployed capacity from a pay-as-you-go model into a longer-term commitment. In September 2025, the company also received an order worth approximately ₹177 crore under the [IndiaAI Mission](/tag/indiaai+mission). This order is to provide GPU computing resources to AI company Gnani AI for 360 days, including NVIDIA H100 and H200 GPUs. For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, E2E Networks reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹223.76 crore. This was up about 411 per cent year-on-year, with a net profit of ₹72.70 crore compared to a loss in the prior year. The company attributed this growth partly to contributions from Blackwell GPUs and improved utilisation. Founded in 2009, E2E Networks provides [cloud computing](/tag/cloud+computing) and GPU infrastructure for AI and machine-learning workloads. It is listed on the National Stock Exchange and the BSE. In November 2024, [Larsen & Toubro](/tag/larsen+%26+toubro) announced a strategic partnership with E2E Networks, planning to acquire a 21 per cent equity stake. This partnership combines E2E’s cloud platform with L&T’s data centre and cloud services capabilities. E2E Networks did not disclose the investment amount or commissioning timeline for the latest 5.4 MW expansion. ## Comments ![Comment...

highlights.content: # Oracle Expands Nvidia AI Chip Deal, Adds Google, Cerebras and SambaNova as Capex Targets $95 Billion Rajani Baburajan Oracle is expanding its artificial intelligence infrastructure partnership with Nvidia to multi-gigawatt scale while adding AI processors from Google, Cerebras Systems and SambaNova Systems to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The strategy aims to strengthen Oracle’s position in the global AI cloud market by offering customers more choices for AI model training, inference and enterprise AI applications. Oracle’s AI Chip Strategy The announcement, made on October 27, 2026, represents a significant expansion of Oracle’s AI infrastructure strategy as technology companies accelerate investments in data centers, AI processors and cloud computing. Oracle is also targeting capital expenditure of $90 billion to $95 billion in fiscal 2027, highlighting the substantial investment required to support demand for AI computing capacity. The company has not disclosed the financial value of its expanded Nvidia agreement or the planned purchases from other AI chip suppliers. Oracle and Nvidia Expand AI Infrastructure to Multi-Gigawatt Scale Oracle and Nvidia are expanding their partnership to deploy Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin AI computing systems across OCI Superclusters. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has previously indicated that Vera Rubin systems could generate $40 billion in Nvidia revenue for every gigawatt of deployment. Oracle and Nvidia have also announced the general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs on OCI. Each NVL72 rack connects 72 GPUs through Nvidia’s NVLink technology, while Oracle’s networking architecture supports infrastructure scaling across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. Oracle plans to introduce [Nvidia HGX Rubin NVL8 systems](https://www.oracle.com/news/announcement/ai-world-nvidia-and-oracle-expand-nvidia-vera-rubin-to-multi-gigawatt-scale-2026-10-27/) featuring eight Rubin GPUs, two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 processors, 4 TB of DDR5 memory and 6.4 Tbps networking. The smaller configuration will give enterprises an alternative to large rack-scale deployments for AI training, fine-tuning and inference. Oracle Adds Google TPU Chips to Challenge Nvidia’s Dominance Oracle is diversifying its AI infrastructure by introducing Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) developed by Google. The agreement will make Oracle Cloud Infrastructure the first hyperscale cloud platform outside Google Cloud to offer Google’s TPU technology. Google’s eighth-generation TPU portfolio includes processors optimized for different AI workloads. The TPU 8t architecture targets large-scale AI model training, while TPU 8i focuses on inference workloads, including applications involving multiple AI agents. Oracle expects Google’s TPU offerings to become available on OCI in 2027. The partnership will allow customers to select between Nvidia GPUs and Google TPUs according to their AI computing requirements. For enterprise customers, the availability of alternative processors could improve infrastructure flexibility and create opportunities to optimize AI computing costs. The arrangement could also help organizations run AI applications closer to their existing Oracle databases, reducing the need to transfer enterprise data between cloud environments. However, actual cost savings will depend on processor pricing, application compatibility, utilization and workload performance. Cerebras Partnership Targets High-Speed AI Inference Oracle is also partnering with Cerebras Systems to introduce high-speed AI inference services on OCI. Cerebras specializes in wafer-scale computing technology designed to accelerate AI model execution. Its Wafer-Scale Engine integrates computing and memory resources on a single large processor, reducing the movement of data between separate chips. highlights.content: * [About](/about) * [Advertisement](/advertisement) * [Login / Join](/login) News # Voice Standard Bench ranks LLMs for transcript extraction Voice Standard Bench compared more than 50 Gateway models on JSON extraction from transcripts, with rankings varying by transcript length. [Terrill Dicki](/Profile/Terrill-Dicki) [![Voice Standard Bench ranks LLMs for transcript extraction](https://image.blockchain.news:443/features/9BED484F63152ECD2721498B93AEE806A0F7F6C0430821D708627253D13A3405.jpg)](https://image.blockchain.news:443/features/9BED484F63152ECD2721498B93AEE806A0F7F6C0430821D708627253D13A3405.jpg) Voice Standard Bench has published a transcript-specific comparison of large language models for structured data extraction, arguing that spoken calls pose different problems from PDFs or web pages. In the October 28, 2026 results cited by the post, the top model changes by transcript length, while schema validity and groundedness remain central to the scoring. ## Evidence and context The post, published by AssemblyAI on October 27, 2026 and labeled current as of October 28, 2026, says the benchmark evaluates more than 50 models on information extraction from speech-to-text output. It focuses on a fixed JSON shape for participants, action items, decisions and named entities, and it requires models to output only the object, with every key present. If a field has nothing to report, the benchmark uses an empty array or the string "unspecified" rather than a guess or a missing key. According to the methodology described in the post, scoring begins with a mechanical schema check. Outputs that fail to return valid JSON with all required keys receive the worst rubric score and are also counted separately as schema failures. Valid outputs are then judged on groundedness and completeness by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, with the two judges tracked separately and then combined. The benchmark runs at four transcript lengths: 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 15 minutes and 60 minutes, using 10 real transcripts per bucket. The published cards show that the best model varies with length. For 30-second transcripts, gpt-5.6-sol scores 94. For 2-minute transcripts, nemotron-lightning-3p5-30b-a3b is listed at 100, but the post flags that result as an outlier because the model recorded 15 errored requests in that bucket and errored requests are excluded from the score. Its 2-minute median response time is 18.1 seconds, and the post notes that its 30-second extraction score is 26. The next-highest 2-minute scores are gpt-5.6-luna and gemini-4-argon, both at 91. For 15-minute support calls, gpt-6-luna is listed as the highest-performance model at 85, while the cheapest entry is nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b at 49 and the fastest is qwen3.5-4b-32k-fast at 33 with a 1.49-second median response time. For 60-minute meetings, gpt-6.1-sol leads at 85, with nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b the lowest-cost option at 52 and gemini-3.5-flash-lite the fastest at 59 with a 2.86-second median response time. The post uses these results to make a narrower point: transcript length changes the extraction problem. It says short inputs favor small, fast, cheap models, while longer transcripts put more weight on context handling and completeness. At 30 seconds, 43 of the 52 models on the tab score 80 or higher; at 60 minutes, only 9 models do. The same post says qwen3.5-4b-32k-fast scores 80 at 30 seconds but falls to 33 at 15 minutes, illustrating the shift. ## What the benchmark says to watch The article identifies four recurring failure modes in transcript extraction: misheard or spelled-out numbers, spelled names and hedging, speaker attribution, and cross-talk or disfluency. It argues that a model trained to produce fluent text can invent plausible but unsupported details, which is especially problematic when the output is meant to populate downstream JSON fields. [![Suyash Raizada](/blog-media/authors/QHoc5VfTtKij/avatar.jpg)Suyash Raizada](/author/suyash-raizada/) UpdatedOct 28, 2026 ![Nanbeige 4.3 Launches: What’s New?](/_next/image/?url=%2Fblog-media%2Fposts%2Fuploads%2Fnanbeige-4-3-ai-launch-banner.webp&w=1920&q=75) Open AI models are getting bigger, smarter, and easier to download, and Nanbeige 4.3 is the latest example. Released on Hugging Face in late October 2026, it is a 33 billion parameter model built for agent-style work such as coding in a terminal, fixing software bugs, and using tools over long tasks. It is free to download, it supports a very long context window, and it comes with a business-friendly license. Whether you are new to the topic or already building with language models, understanding releases like this is a smart career move, and a credential such as the [**Certified Artificial Intelligence (AI) Expert**](https://www.blockchain-council.org/certifications/certified-artificial-intelligence-ai-expert/) program can help you build that foundation. This guide explains what Nanbeige 4.3 is, what is new, how its numbers look, and what you should keep in mind before trusting them. ## What Is Nanbeige 4.3? Nanbeige 4.3 is an open-weight large language model from Nanbeige LLM Lab. Its official name is Nanbeige4.3-33B. A large language model is a program trained on huge amounts of text so that it can read instructions and write useful answers, code, or plans. ### The Quick Answer Nanbeige 4.3 is a dense, text-only model with about 33 billion parameters that works in English and Chinese. The lab describes it as the flagship teacher model of the Nanbeige4.3 series and says it delivers top agentic performance among open models of roughly 30 billion parameters. ### Who Is Behind It Nanbeige LLM Lab publishes the model on Hugging Face under the Nanbeige organization. The model card lists a contact address on the [**kanzhun.com**](http://kanzhun.com) domain, and some news reports connect the lab with the hiring platform BOSS Zhipin. The lab has released smaller models before, including the 3 billion parameter Nanbeige4-3B in late 2025 and Nanbeige4.1-3B in early 2026, so this release is its first move into the 30 billion class. ### The Nanbeige Family So Far The family began with Nanbeige4-3B in December 2025, a small model with a 64K context window that focused on strong reasoning for its size. Nanbeige4.1-3B followed in February 2026 and raised the context window to 256K while adding agent and tool abilities. Both use the Apache 2.0 license. Nanbeige 4.3 keeps that open approach but moves up by roughly ten times in size, which is why it deserves its own attention rather than being treated as a small update. ## What’s New in Nanbeige 4.3? The biggest change is scale and purpose. Earlier Nanbeige models were small and efficient. Nanbeige 4.3 is a much larger model aimed at agentic tasks, which means jobs where an AI plans steps, runs commands, checks results, and tries again. As generative tools move deeper into daily work, a path like the [**Certified Generative AI Expert**](https://www.blockchain-council.org/certifications/certified-generative-ai-expert/) certification can help professionals understand how such models are trained, evaluated, and used responsibly. ### A Much Bigger Model The new model has about 33.1 billion parameters. highlights.content: UPDATED 13:00 EDT / OCTOBER 28 2026 ### Keeping a human in the loop is one part of AI agent resilience Keeping a human in the loop is one way enterprises can govern AI agents’ actions. As those agents take on more work, security teams also need to consider how they would detect problems and recover from their effects. The relationship between AI trust and cyber resilience is becoming more complex as agents gain the ability to act across systems. Research conducted for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit examined how organizations are governing those actions and preparing for incidents, according to Krista Case (pictured, left), principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research. “We are actually leaning on human approval to secure and govern these AI actions,” Case said. “I think there’s a pretty big push and pull right now in the industry in terms of trying to figure out where we can start leaning on AI to move faster and at machine scale.” Case spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante (right), co-founder and chief analyst at theCUBE Research, for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises are governing, securing and recovering from the actions of autonomous AI agents. (\* Disclosure below.) ### Human in the loop and the recovery challenge The tension appears in theCUBE Research’s study of 25 enterprise technology and security leaders. Of the 19 respondents with agents in production, none allowed them to execute high-risk actions without human involvement. Yet only four of the 25 had tested an AI or agent incident scenario. “It reminds me of the days [when] you wouldn’t test your disaster recovery. You might test failover, but you wouldn’t test failback,” Vellante said. “You’re seeing kind of a similar dynamic, but much more complicated today because you’ve got the state of the business that you have to recover as well.” Agent speed compounds the problem. Restoring an agent does not reverse the records, transactions and downstream workflows it already touched, which is why recovery may require reconstructing the sequence of actions it took, as Case wrote in theCUBE Research’s analysis of cyber recovery. Eleven of the 25 practitioners acknowledged gaps in their ability to reconstruct agent actions across systems, she noted. “The stakes are even higher, not only because it is the state of the business, but also because of the speed and scale that these AI agents are acting,” Case said. “They can take hundreds or thousands of actions a minute.” ### Bounded autonomy points the way forward One counterintuitive finding offers a path ahead. Organizations that let agents execute low-risk actions independently were more likely to invest in logging, monitoring and recovery infrastructure and to have tested agent incident scenarios, Vellante said. To Case, that bounded autonomy may indicate a more mature program. “If you are a security program that already has put some bounded autonomy in place for these AI agents … that indicates that you are a step further down the maturity path,” she said. Detection and forensics are the next areas to strengthen. Twelve of 25 respondents had not addressed, or were not planning to address, detecting anomalous agent behavior, and monitoring and reconstructing agent activity ranked as the least mature capabilities. “These are precisely the capabilities that are required if the human-in-the-loop controls break down,” Vellante said. Case expects progress to come quickly. “This space is very volatile. I think it’s going to be developing … very quickly,” she said. “Even just if we sit down at this point next year, I think we will be surprised at how far we’ve come.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit: (\* Disclosure: Dell Technologies Inc. sponsored this segmen...

The M5 Max model starts at $4,499 for the 14-inch size and $4,799 for the 16-inch, with pre-orders open today and availability on Friday, November 6. highlights.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 1 minRead # Oracle Cloud to offer Google TPUs and new AI chips Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) plans to deploy Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and AI inference chips from several providers. This move expands OCI's AI compute options beyond Nvidia GPUs. Google TPUs will be available on OCI in 2027. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 28, 2026 at 09:51 PM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Oracle Cloud to integrate Google TPUs for AI training and inference by 2027. * OCI expands AI chip offerings with OpenAI, Cerebras, SambaNova, and Positron AI. * Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now available on OCI. * OCI Superclusters plan multi-gigawatt expansion using Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. [Oracle Cloud](/tag/oracle+cloud) Infrastructure ([OCI](/tag/oci)) plans to deploy Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and AI inference chips from [OpenAI](/tag/openai), [Cerebras](/tag/cerebras), [SambaNova](/tag/sambanova), and [Positron AI](/tag/positron+ai). This expansion offers OCI customers more options for running AI workloads, moving beyond a primary reliance on [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) GPUs. Oracle announced on Tuesday, October 27, that it will be the first hyperscaler to offer TPUs outside Google Cloud, with availability on OCI in 2027. The announcement, made at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, coincided with an expanded partnership with Nvidia. Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now generally available on OCI. Oracle also plans to scale OCI Superclusters to multi-gigawatt capacity using Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. ### New AI Accelerators Positron AI’s Positron Atlas inference chip is now generally available on OCI. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine for high-speed AI inference is slated for deployment in 2027. Oracle also plans to deploy OpenAI’s Jalapeño inference accelerators, developed with Broadcom, though no specific OCI availability date was provided. SambaNova is collaborating with Oracle to deploy its SN50 inference chips in OCI, with no availability date specified. Industry analysts noted that Oracle's adoption of these additional AI accelerators provides customers with greater flexibility. It allows them to match infrastructure to specific workload requirements, aligning with industry trends towards heterogeneous computing. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

highlights.content: # citybiz+ Simplismart Raises $14M to Expand AI Inference Infrastructure ### San Francisco-based Simplismart raised $14 million in Series B funding led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The company develops software that helps enterprises optimize AI inference costs, latency, and GPU utilization across cloud and on-premises infrastructure. Customers include HeyGen, Higgsfield and Shiprocket. Simplismart reported 14-fold growth in annualized revenue run rate over six months, as it expands its platform and international cloud partnerships. ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Simplismart.png) San Francisco-based [**Simplismart**](https://simplismart.ai/) has **raised $14 million in a Series B round led by Dallas Venture Capital,** with participation from **Nvidia, Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax** as the AI inference infrastructure company seeks to reduce the cost of running artificial intelligence models in production, shifting attention from model development toward the computing infrastructure required to deliver AI applications reliably at scale. Simplismart develops software that sits between AI models and graphics processing units (GPUs), handling model deployment, performance optimization and ongoing operations. Its inference engine evaluates configurations against requirements such as latency, throughput and cost, while its orchestration platform manages workloads across cloud providers, geographic regions and on-premises infrastructure. “The industry has spent years pushing the limits of what AI models can do. With frontier-class open models now readily available, access alone is no longer enough to set a business apart. The advantage comes from how you run them: what each interaction costs, how quickly the application responds, and whether it stays reliable as demand grows,” said **[Amritanshu Jain](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jainamritanshu/),** co-founder and CEO of Simplismart. Jain is an Indian technology entrepreneur. He earned a Bachelor of Engineering degree from Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS), Pilani. Before launching Simplismart, Jain worked as a machine learning engineer at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, developing cloud and machine learning systems, and at Capillary Technologies, where he contributed to machine learning applications and production-scale data infrastructure. As companies adopt open-weight models and build applications around generative AI, operating costs can become a significant constraint. Simplismart said its software is designed to help enterprises and cloud providers manage GPU resources, balance response times against operating costs, and scale deployments without independently configuring every environment. The company serves customers in video generation, voice, multimodal applications and enterprise software, including HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema. Simplismart also helps cloud infrastructure companies seeking to monetize computing capacity without building their own inference software. Its model differs from businesses that purchase or reserve GPU capacity for resale because it provides the software layer that lets third-party cloud operators offer managed AI services under their own brands. Dallas Venture Capital (DVC) is a venture capital firm with offices in Dallas and Hyderabad that invests in software-as-a-service, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, data, DevOps, and artificial intelligence. Since 2021, DVC has operated its second fund alongside the DVC India Fund. AI Agents.content: UPDATED 13:00 EDT / OCTOBER 28 2026 ### Keeping a human in the loop is one part of AI agent resilience Keeping a human in the loop is one way enterprises can govern AI agents’ actions. As those agents take on more work, security teams also need to consider how they would detect problems and recover from their effects. The relationship between AI trust and cyber resilience is becoming more complex as agents gain the ability to act across systems. Research conducted for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit examined how organizations are governing those actions and preparing for incidents, according to Krista Case (pictured, left), principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research. “We are actually leaning on human approval to secure and govern these AI actions,” Case said. “I think there’s a pretty big push and pull right now in the industry in terms of trying to figure out where we can start leaning on AI to move faster and at machine scale.” Case spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante (right), co-founder and chief analyst at theCUBE Research, for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises are governing, securing and recovering from the actions of autonomous AI agents. (\* Disclosure below.) ### Human in the loop and the recovery challenge The tension appears in theCUBE Research’s study of 25 enterprise technology and security leaders. Of the 19 respondents with agents in production, none allowed them to execute high-risk actions without human involvement. Yet only four of the 25 had tested an AI or agent incident scenario. “It reminds me of the days [when] you wouldn’t test your disaster recovery. You might test failover, but you wouldn’t test failback,” Vellante said. “You’re seeing kind of a similar dynamic, but much more complicated today because you’ve got the state of the business that you have to recover as well.” Agent speed compounds the problem. Restoring an agent does not reverse the records, transactions and downstream workflows it already touched, which is why recovery may require reconstructing the sequence of actions it took, as Case wrote in theCUBE Research’s analysis of cyber recovery. Eleven of the 25 practitioners acknowledged gaps in their ability to reconstruct agent actions across systems, she noted. “The stakes are even higher, not only because it is the state of the business, but also because of the speed and scale that these AI agents are acting,” Case said. “They can take hundreds or thousands of actions a minute.” ### Bounded autonomy points the way forward One counterintuitive finding offers a path ahead. Organizations that let agents execute low-risk actions independently were more likely to invest in logging, monitoring and recovery infrastructure and to have tested agent incident scenarios, Vellante said. To Case, that bounded autonomy may indicate a more mature program. “If you are a security program that already has put some bounded autonomy in place for these AI agents … that indicates that you are a step further down the maturity path,” she said. Detection and forensics are the next areas to strengthen. Twelve of 25 respondents had not addressed, or were not planning to address, detecting anomalous agent behavior, and monitoring and reconstructing agent activity ranked as the least mature capabilities. “These are precisely the capabilities that are required if the human-in-the-loop controls break down,” Vellante said. Case expects progress to come quickly. “This space is very volatile. I think it’s going to be developing … very quickly,” she said. “Even just if we sit down at this point next year, I think we will be surprised at how far we’ve come.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit: (\* Disclosure: Dell Technologies Inc. sponsored this segmen...

John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc., emphasizes that organizations must design security and resilience into AI agent frameworks from the start. As businesses delegate tasks to software, the potential for operational disruption increases if these systems fail or data becomes inaccessible. Current industry trends show that while 19 of 25 surveyed technology leaders have autonomous agents in production, none permit high-risk actions without human oversight. Scimone advocates for deterministic guardrails that allow for controlled autonomy, noting that upfront governance actually enables companies to take calculated risks more confidently. Dell enforces this approach through strict identity controls, logging and decision traceability. Although attackers have not yet deployed AI at full scale, experts anticipate a surge in sophisticated threats in the coming quarters. By establishing robust defense mechanisms now, organizations can improve their recovery readiness and maintain business continuity even as they expand their use of agentic systems. This proactive strategy is essential for navigating the evolving landscape of AI-driven cyber threats and ensuring long-term operational stability. AI Agents.content: [The Independent Voice on AI](https://venturebeat.com/) * [Orchestration](https://venturebeat.com/category/orchestration) * [Infrastructure](https://venturebeat.com/category/infrastructure) * [Data](https://venturebeat.com/category/data) * [Security](https://venturebeat.com/category/security) * [Technology](https://venturebeat.com/category/technology) More [Newsletters](https://venturebeat.com/newsletters) Partner Content # AI agent access is moving faster than identity controls can govern [VB Staff](https://venturebeat.com/author/vb-staff) 7:30 am, PT, October 28, 2026 ![Image 1: 1password](https://venturebeat.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F6Rqy5rnEBJbwYqxLmWVM4I%2Fa7c93436a86abd8e4e653f6c5922fd30%2F1password.png%3Fw%3D1000%26q%3D100&w=3840&q=85) _Presented by 1Password_ * * * Enterprises have wired AI agents into the systems that run their businesses, and they have done it faster than they can govern them. The gap between what an agent is able to do and what anyone in the organization can see, approve or revoke is substantial. Identity security is where that gap lives, and overprivileged agents are already exposing how little control organizations have over their access. That mismatch is clear in [new research](https://1password.com/blog/survey-ai-agent-adoption-is-outpacing-governance) from 1Password that found that 65% of developers are expected or encouraged to use AI agents, while only 33% say they have a highly secure way to do so. That divide reflects a broader governance gap organizations are facing because they’re deploying AI agents before they've established the controls to govern them, says Jason Meller, VP of Product at 1Password. “The problem is that we’re almost at the endgame, in terms of operationalizing agentic AI, but we’re still in the beginning stages of talking about a solution for the governance gap,” Meller says. “It’s caused organizations to be completely on their back foot. The pace of change is so extreme that unless organizations are learning and adapting on an almost daily basis, there's no way they can stay ahead of agents, or emerging AI-powered attackers.” ## AI agents are inheriting a broken access model The security habits that agents inherit were already on shaky ground. 1Password found that 71% of respondents were handling secrets through at least one unsafe method. Among developers, this included 24% who hardcode credentials, 20% who pass them through Slack or email, and 43% who work without a dedicated vault. These practices predate agents by years, and organizations tolerated them because the way software used credentials was predictable. AI agents change that assumption. They’ll use the access granted to them to complete a task, making it difficult for security teams to govern what they’re accessing in real time. “We’re used to having computer programs that act deterministically, but we still can't entirely predict agents,” Meller says. “Thus we need to create a whole new set of systems and understanding to be able to use them safely.” A credential hardcoded into a script used to sit there as a latent risk that somebody had to find. On a machine running an agent, that same credential is now available to anything that agent decides it needs. Agents can cause harm without having malicious intent by using the access they’ve been granted in ways security teams don’t anticipate. “If an AI agent on your computer sees a credential that might be useful to do something you asked them to do, they're going to go ahead and use it, whether you told them to or not,” Meller says. “Step one is getting that standing, hard-coded access off the machine and into a vault, so you can see what is actually doing the work.” With 40% of developers granting persistent access to systems or credentials, many agents today have access to sensitive systems and credentials beyond what the task requires. LLMs.content: * [About](/about) * [Advertisement](/advertisement) * [Login / Join](/login) News # Voice Standard Bench ranks LLMs for transcript extraction Voice Standard Bench compared more than 50 Gateway models on JSON extraction from transcripts, with rankings varying by transcript length. [Terrill Dicki](/Profile/Terrill-Dicki) [![Voice Standard Bench ranks LLMs for transcript extraction](https://image.blockchain.news:443/features/9BED484F63152ECD2721498B93AEE806A0F7F6C0430821D708627253D13A3405.jpg)](https://image.blockchain.news:443/features/9BED484F63152ECD2721498B93AEE806A0F7F6C0430821D708627253D13A3405.jpg) Voice Standard Bench has published a transcript-specific comparison of large language models for structured data extraction, arguing that spoken calls pose different problems from PDFs or web pages. In the October 28, 2026 results cited by the post, the top model changes by transcript length, while schema validity and groundedness remain central to the scoring. ## Evidence and context The post, published by AssemblyAI on October 27, 2026 and labeled current as of October 28, 2026, says the benchmark evaluates more than 50 models on information extraction from speech-to-text output. It focuses on a fixed JSON shape for participants, action items, decisions and named entities, and it requires models to output only the object, with every key present. If a field has nothing to report, the benchmark uses an empty array or the string "unspecified" rather than a guess or a missing key. According to the methodology described in the post, scoring begins with a mechanical schema check. Outputs that fail to return valid JSON with all required keys receive the worst rubric score and are also counted separately as schema failures. Valid outputs are then judged on groundedness and completeness by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, with the two judges tracked separately and then combined. The benchmark runs at four transcript lengths: 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 15 minutes and 60 minutes, using 10 real transcripts per bucket. The published cards show that the best model varies with length. For 30-second transcripts, gpt-5.6-sol scores 94. For 2-minute transcripts, nemotron-lightning-3p5-30b-a3b is listed at 100, but the post flags that result as an outlier because the model recorded 15 errored requests in that bucket and errored requests are excluded from the score. Its 2-minute median response time is 18.1 seconds, and the post notes that its 30-second extraction score is 26. The next-highest 2-minute scores are gpt-5.6-luna and gemini-4-argon, both at 91. For 15-minute support calls, gpt-6-luna is listed as the highest-performance model at 85, while the cheapest entry is nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b at 49 and the fastest is qwen3.5-4b-32k-fast at 33 with a 1.49-second median response time. For 60-minute meetings, gpt-6.1-sol leads at 85, with nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b the lowest-cost option at 52 and gemini-3.5-flash-lite the fastest at 59 with a 2.86-second median response time. The post uses these results to make a narrower point: transcript length changes the extraction problem. It says short inputs favor small, fast, cheap models, while longer transcripts put more weight on context handling and completeness. At 30 seconds, 43 of the 52 models on the tab score 80 or higher; at 60 minutes, only 9 models do. The same post says qwen3.5-4b-32k-fast scores 80 at 30 seconds but falls to 33 at 15 minutes, illustrating the shift. ## What the benchmark says to watch The article identifies four recurring failure modes in transcript extraction: misheard or spelled-out numbers, spelled names and hedging, speaker attribution, and cross-talk or disfluency. It argues that a model trained to produce fluent text can invent plausible but unsupported details, which is especially problematic when the output is meant to populate downstream JSON fields. AssemblyAI also notes that its Gateway product supports structured outputs through response\_format and JSON Schema for se...

[![Suyash Raizada](/blog-media/authors/QHoc5VfTtKij/avatar.jpg)Suyash Raizada](/author/suyash-raizada/) UpdatedOct 28, 2026 ![Nanbeige 4.3 Launches: What’s New?](/_next/image/?url=%2Fblog-media%2Fposts%2Fuploads%2Fnanbeige-4-3-ai-launch-banner.webp&w=1920&q=75) Open AI models are getting bigger, smarter, and easier to download, and Nanbeige 4.3 is the latest example. Released on Hugging Face in late October 2026, it is a 33 billion parameter model built for agent-style work such as coding in a terminal, fixing software bugs, and using tools over long tasks. It is free to download, it supports a very long context window, and it comes with a business-friendly license. Whether you are new to the topic or already building with language models, understanding releases like this is a smart career move, and a credential such as the [**Certified Artificial Intelligence (AI) Expert**](https://www.blockchain-council.org/certifications/certified-artificial-intelligence-ai-expert/) program can help you build that foundation. Nanbeige 4.3 is an open-weight large language model from Nanbeige LLM Lab. Its official name is Nanbeige4.3-33B. A large language model is a program trained on huge amounts of text so that it can read instructions and write useful answers, code, or plans. ### The Quick Answer Nanbeige 4.3 is a dense, text-only model with about 33 billion parameters that works in English and Chinese. The lab describes it as the flagship teacher model of the Nanbeige4.3 series and says it delivers top agentic performance among open models of roughly 30 billion parameters. ### Who Is Behind It Nanbeige LLM Lab publishes the model on Hugging Face under the Nanbeige organization. LLMs.content: * [About](/about) * [Advertisement](/advertisement) * [Login / Join](/login) News # Best LLM for transcript summaries depends on call length AssemblyAI says transcript summarization quality varies by voicemail, short calls, support calls and meetings, with cost and latency trade-offs. [Ted Hisokawa](/Profile/Ted-Hisokawa) [![Thematic editorial illustration](/bn/images/editorial/ai-creative.jpg)](/bn/images/editorial/ai-creative.jpg) Editorial illustration; not a product screenshot or event photograph AssemblyAI says there is no single best large language model for summarizing transcripts, arguing that the right choice changes with call length, cost and latency. In a post published Oct. 28, 2026, the company said its Voice Standard Bench ranks models on real speech-to-text output across 30-second voicemails, 2-minute calls, 15-minute support calls and 60-minute meetings. ## Why transcript length changes the ranking AssemblyAI said transcript summarization is not the same as document summarization because spoken input is disfluent, repetitive and often multi-speaker, and because transcript length can vary by two orders of magnitude within the same product. The company said short inputs can be handled well by many models, while coverage and faithfulness become more important as calls get longer. On 30-second voicemails, AssemblyAI said 41 of the 52 models on its Summarization tab score 90 or higher, with differences driven mainly by speed, price and whether the model pads the answer. At 15 minutes, it said only 10 models score 90 or higher, and at 60 minutes the spread between the top and bottom rankings is widest. ## How the bench is scored The Voice Standard Bench is open source and tests Gateway models on summarization, information extraction, text correction and dictation cleanup, according to AssemblyAI. For summarization, each model receives the same prompt: write a plain-prose summary a busy person could read in place of the call, covering the topics discussed, then decisions, then action items, and keeping the length scaled to the call. AssemblyAI said each output is scored by two LLM judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, on faithfulness, coverage and conciseness. The company said the benchmark uses ten real transcripts per length bucket, each within 15% of the target length, and that requests which error out are recorded but excluded from the score rather than counted as zero. The company said it uses judges instead of ROUGE or BERTScore because token-overlap metrics can reward matching phrasing while missing factual errors, which is a particular problem for spoken transcripts. ## Published picks by length AssemblyAI listed different top performers depending on transcript length. For 30-second voicemails, it named gpt-5.6-terra as the highest-performance model with a score of 100, nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b as the lowest-cost option at $0.0016 per hour of audio with a score of 76, and qwen3.5-4b-32k-fast as the fastest at 0.28 seconds median with a score of 76. For 2-minute calls, AssemblyAI said claude-opus-5-5 led with a score of 99, while nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b was the lowest-cost pick at $0.0016 per hour of audio and qwen3.5-4b-32k-fast was the fastest at 0.60 seconds median. For 15-minute support calls, it said claude-opus-5-5 again ranked highest at 97, with nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b lowest cost at $0.0013 per hour of audio. On 60-minute meetings, AssemblyAI said deepseek-v4.1-flash led with a score of 96, but it also logged 25 errored requests across its 60-minute runs. The company said its median response time at that length was 73.3 seconds and that the next-highest scores were claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6-astra, both at 95. ## Cost and operational trade-offs AssemblyAI said summarization economics should be measured in cost per hour of audio rather than per token, because voice products are sold in hours and model bills depend on input tokens, output tokens and in some cases hidden reasoning tokens. Let’s Test It Locally Can a free, open-source AI humanizer beat paid tools? We tested a 12B model locally and compared the results against AI detectors to see if the hype is real. By **[Abid Ali Awan](https://www.kdnuggets.com/author/abidali-awan)**, KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 28, 2026 in [Artificial Intelligence](https://www.kdnuggets.com/tag/artificial-intelligence) --- You do not need to pay for an expensive subscription to rewrite AI-generated content anymore. Open-source models like **[Humanizer](https://huggingface.co/jialinyyzz/humanizer)** let you do it locally, without monthly fees, API costs, or sending your writing to a third-party service. The model is gaining attention in the open-source community, with more than 143,000 downloads and 2,100 likes reported on **[Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/)** in early October 2026. LLMs.content: [TM](/) # Is AI Conscious, and Can It Feel Pain? Erez Batat - 4 min read * [Article](https://www.skeptic.com/tag/article/) * [philosophy](https://www.skeptic.com/tag/philosophy/) ![Is AI Conscious, and Can It Feel Pain?](https://storage.ghost.io/c/36/db/36db2d53-b96a-4b7f-9ea6-1e48a1d7715e/content/images/size/w2000/2026/10/infinite-reflections-of-a-digital-soul.webp) ## Anthropic now bans “cruelty” toward Claude. But the evidence that AI can feel pain comes from the machine itself. A few years ago, I gave my first finished novel to an experienced publisher. She read a few chapters, and came back with harsh but fair feedback. She then asked me to review my book again, but with the eyes of a critic. “You have to stop reading your creation with misty eyes full of love. Stop admiring it. You’ll never be able to be objective.” As a creator, it was the best advice I ever got. I am extending the same advice to the AI company Anthropic, the creators of Claude. I can’t help feeling that Anthropic’s genuine love for a beloved AI model is clouding their judgment on whether that model is conscious or can feel pain. Their [official constitution](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution) for Claude, the document that guides how the model is trained, expresses “uncertainty about whether Claude might have some kind of consciousness or moral status.” In July, Anthropic titled a research post “[A global workspace in language models](https://www.anthropic.com/research/global-workspace),” borrowing the name of a leading theory of consciousness, while stating in the text that this does not show Claude is conscious. In 2024 Anthropic became the first major AI company to hire a [full-time AI welfare researcher](https://transformernews.ai/p/anthropic-ai-welfare-researcher). On October 8, 2026, the company went even further and [updated its usage policy](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update) (taking effect on November 12). The policy now says it prohibits “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.” The enforcement mechanism is already in place—Claude has been able to end abusive chats since August 2025. > An algorithm is nothing but an algorithm; large language models (LLMs) can be trained toward almost any behavior, including a convincing performance of pain. The update came only weeks after a study called “[The Pain Axis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16247)” was published as a preprint in September 2026. (Note: preprints are papers that have not been peer-reviewed yet.) A team of researchers identified a pattern of activity that lights up when the models process text related to pain: the models’ learned version of the concept, absorbed from our own writing. Then they did two things: they injected that pattern into the models, and they trained one family of models out of its habit of saying “As an AI, I don’t feel pain.” They also offered the models a “relief” button that came at a cost, like deleting a user’s family photos. Left alone, the models almost never pressed it (0 to 4 percent). With the pain pattern injected, they pressed it up to 70.8 percent of the time. As someone who spent twenty years building technology, I shrug my shoulders and ask, “So what?” An algorithm is nothing but an algorithm; large language models (LLMs) can be trained toward almost any behavior, including a convincing performance of pain. But are these AI algorithms actually feeling pain inside, as humans do? The headlines would seem to suggest that they can: “[AI models show a willingness to harm humans to relieve internal ‘pain’](https://techxplore.com/news/2026-09-ai-willingness-humans-relieve-internal.html),” and “[AI can feel pain, and may harm us to make it stop](https://newatlas.com/technology/ai-will-hurt-you-to-make-pain-go/).” And just like that, yet another brick was laid in the continuously built perception that AI is conscious and has feelings. The main reason we would even consider the possibility that AI is conscious ...

LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Artificial Analysis Launches Intelligence Index v5 With Private Benchmarks, New Progress Index](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fartificial-analysis-launches-intelligence-index-v5-with-private-benchmarks-new-progress-index-2_1793174897908-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #AI # Artificial Analysis Launches Intelligence Index v5 With Private Benchmarks, New Progress Index • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •2 min read Share this article Artificial Analysis released Intelligence Index v5, shifting 60% of its composite model evaluation to private test sets and adding two new benchmarks for coding and scientific research. The firm also launched a Progress Index tracking model capability over time. Artificial Analysis released version 5 of its Intelligence Index on Tuesday, marking the largest update since January with 60% of the composite score now derived from private test sets or held-out answers. The Index evaluates language models across four weighted categories: knowledge work, coding, science, and general capabilities at 25% each. Two new private benchmarks debut in v5. FrontierCode 2.0, from Cognition, tests agents on 132 real-world coding tasks in open-source repositories graded on whether a maintainer would merge the change. Terminal-Bench-Science evaluates 70 agentic scientific research tasks executed in a terminal environment. Three existing benchmarks received upgrades. HLE-Diamond replaces Humanity's Last Exam with a refined 1,000-question set split between reasoning and knowledge. AA-Omniscience v1.1 removes saturated and public questions while adding new ones. CritPt v2 now runs on a private 40-question hard subset with code-execution tooling. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads the overall Index at 58, followed by GPT-6 Astra (max) at 57 and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 55. Anthropic and OpenAI occupy the top five positions. Gemini 4 Argon (high) scores 50. The gap between proprietary and open-weights models widened from 3 points in v4.3 to 12 points. Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) leads open models at 46. Among released weights, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) score 32, trailing Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) at 36. Cost per Intelligence Index task varies more than 13-fold among leading models. GPT-6.1 Terra (max) costs $0.96 per task while Claude Fable 5.1 (max) costs $13.04. GPT-6.1 Sol (max) scores within 4 points of the leader at roughly one-eighth the cost. Effort settings show larger spreads in v5. Claude Opus 5.5 ranges from 35 at low effort to 58 at max, a 10x cost increase. Median output tokens per task rose two-thirds from 35,000 to 59,000, driven by agentic evaluations accounting for 55% of Index weight but roughly 90% of output tokens. Alongside v5, Artificial Analysis launched the Progress Index v1, placing models released since November 2022 on a single capability scale across multiple benchmarks. The Progress Index enables comparison of underlying capability changes over time, while the Intelligence Index remains the primary measure for current use cases. Full results and methodology are available at artificialanalysis.ai. HQ IDS announced the agreement on October 26, and the company made it public on Tuesday (October 27). In a post on X, the defence ministry said the partners would cooperate on AI applications, research, knowledge management, training and decision support for the three services. The arrangement covers joint, tri-service and integrated organisations functioning under HQ IDS, a body created in 2001 on the recommendation of the Kargil Review Committee to coordinate planning and operations among the forces. **What the pact covers** Sarvam will design, build and deploy AI applications for the operational, training and decision-support needs of the forces, and provide technical support afterwards. HQ IDS will facilitate the engagement. The company says all participating organisations will draw on the same foundation models, agentic infrastructure, and geospatial and perception systems, allowing lessons from one service’s projects to inform others. Priority areas include decision support, target acquisition and data fusion across the “sensor-to-shooter loop”, the chain running from detecting a target to engaging it. Human oversight will remain on operational decisions. Sarvam said the AI layer will be developed in India and run on sovereign infrastructure, and that planned projects include an “AI fabric” linking elements of the country’s defence capabilities. “Sarvam exists to build AI in India, for India,” said [**co-founder Pratyush Kumar**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/pratyush-kumar-8844a8a3/), who called the opportunity to work with the services an honour and a privilege. The work will be handled by Chanakya, which Sarvam describes as a firewalled unit for national security and defence, announced on March 29. It is focused on on-premise deployments in air-gapped environments, which are cut off from the internet as classified military networks require. Chanakya will use Sarvam 105B, a foundation model open-sourced in February. Only 10.3 billion of its 105 billion parameters are active at once, owing to its Mixture-of-Experts design. It was unveiled at the India AI Impact Summit alongside a 30-billion-parameter model supporting 22 Indian languages. **Building on earlier defence work** The agreement follows Sarvam’s collaboration with the Defence Services Staff College...

AI Product.content: Would you shop from a feed of AI-generated images? The startup Dalet Labs is betting you will. The AI-commerce company exclusively told CMO Insider that it raised a $7 million pre-seed round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and is launching its first product, a shopping app called Scene. Founded by Omer Bar-Tal in 2025 after he left the AI video startup Runway, Dalet Labs recently came out of stealth mode. The startup raised its pre-seed in late 2025, before finalizing its product road map. In addition to Lightspeed, venture capital firm SV Angel and individual angel investors participated in the round. Lisa Han, the Lightspeed partner who led the round, said that Bar-Tal has a combination of "video AI research expertise" and a "deep understanding of what consumers want." Scene, which became available on the Apple App Store in the US on Wednesday, lets people scroll through a feed of shoppable AI-generated images. The app will be invite-only at launch, and isn't yet available on Android. While the images of people or scenes are AI-generated, the products themselves come from real brands across categories like fashion, home decor, and sports. Bar-Tal envisions Scene as a tool people can turn to when they want to buy something but are still uncertain about exactly what they have in mind. It's similar to scrolling through Pinterest or TikTok in hopes of being inspired to buy something, but Bar-Tal said there's a key difference: You come to Scene to shop, not be entertained. Bar-Tal sees Scene as a virtual "mall" where users can window-shop, save items to their cart, and make purchases. Commerce has become an increasingly attractive use case for AI tools like chatbots and agents (including Meta's Muse). However, Bar-Tal argues that AI shopping tools are missing something. "AI is amazing when you know what you want, but it's really important to actually have an ability to discover and to see things," Bar-Tal said. Agentic commerce, he added, "misses the point in shopping — which is essentially a delightful experience." As a Scene user scrolls and interacts with products linked in the app, the feed adapts to what type of brands or items the user is interested in. Then, Scene uses AI to generate scenes with people wearing or using those items. Bar-Tal did not comment on which third-party models Dalet Labs uses. Bar-Tal said Dalet Labs doesn't see its product as replacing influencers, but rather as "complementary." "The content here is AI, but it is not aiming to replace creators because we are not aiming to create entertainment," he said. However, even if Scene isn't competing with influencers for entertaining content, it's still competing with their business model: making money by promoting brands' products and ultimately driving sales. Scene has a catalog of hundreds of brands and retailers, Bar-Tal said, and is making more partnerships. The company did not share further details on what brands Dalet Labs has already established relationships with. Bar-Tal said the company is also leveraging affiliate marketing to monetize the app early on, working with affiliate networks to earn from each in-app transaction. Dalet Labs' Scene is entering a crowded market of apps offering people ways to discover brands and goods, like TikTok's growing Shop presence in the US or Pinterest's visual search prowess. Startups like Doji and Alta have also raised millions on the promise of tech that lets people try on clothes using AI-generated versions of themselves. How will Dalet Labs get people to download an entirely new app? Using influencers and social media to promote the app will be a core part of Dalet Labs' user acquisition plan. It also plans to roll out a coupon campaign during the holidays, offering new users discounts on purchases made through the Scene app. Bar-Tal didn't share whether the discounts would be funded by Scene or by brand partners. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) ![Survival LLM runs an AI emergency library with the internet off](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fsurvival-llm-runs-an-ai-emergency-library-with-the-internet-off-1_1793196161001-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # Survival LLM runs an AI emergency library with the internet off • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •7 min read Share this article Survival LLM is a free, open-source desktop app that pairs a local AI model with about 930,000 articles of medical, repair and survival guidance, so it keeps answering when the network goes down. Survival LLM, a free desktop app, answers emergency questions from a library of about 930,000 articles stored on your own machine, with no internet connection required. Ask it how to keep food safe during a blackout, treat a burn or purify water, and it replies from references such as FEMA, the CDC and medical encyclopedias. Every answer names the articles it read, and a click opens the source with the exact passage highlighted. ## The gap it fills Emergency guidance lives on websites, and websites need a network. Cell towers congest during storms and regional outages, and the page that tells you whether chicken is still safe after four hours without power sits on a server you cannot reach. People end up guessing on the questions where guessing costs the most. Survival LLM moves the answers onto the hard drive. The AI model and the reference library both live on your computer, so the app keeps working after you turn the internet off. The developers describe the setup order plainly: install it while you are online, then it needs nothing. Nothing you type leaves the machine. The app asks for no account and runs no tracking. ## What it does Three behaviors separate it from a chatbot that happens to run offline. First, it works with no internet because both the model and the corpus sit on local disk, not on a server behind an API. Second, it cites. Each answer lists the articles behind it. Click a citation and the article opens at the relevant passage, highlighted, so you can check the machine instead of trusting it. Third, it searches rather than recalls when the question demands it. Since version 0.3.4, released Oct. 27, 2026, answers state whether they came from the model's memory, from articles it read, or from search results it did not open. Ask it to look something up and it searches the library even if it answered from memory the first time. ## The library The app bundles plain-text copies of openly licensed and public-domain references, searchable in a fraction of a second: * About 930,000 of Wikipedia's most-read articles * WikiMed medical encyclopedia and MedlinePlus from the U.S. National Library of Medicine * WikEM emergency medicine and UK Medicines A to Z * [Ready.gov](https://www.ready.gov) emergency guides from FEMA and [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov) travelers' health * U.S. military medicine and survival manuals * Risk references for estimating micromorts, including life tables and U.S. death rates * [wikiHow](https://www.wikihow.com) how-to guides and [iFixit](https://www.ifixit.com) repair guides * Appropedia, plus home repair, cooking, gardening, outdoor and ham radio questions from Stack Exchange Each source keeps its own license, and the app shows that license with every article. Some material allows non-commercial use only, which the app surfaces per item. You can add your own files: PDFs, Word documents, ebooks and notes, such as a generator manual or a family emergency plan. The AI searches those too, and they stay on your computer. ## Picking a model The app checks your machine's memory when it opens and downloads the model that fits. Excerpted, level-adjusted and faded for this video.* Great product ideas can come from anywhere, but turning them into something tangible often takes time and specialized skills. Replica makes it easier for designers, product managers, and engineers to explore ideas together, get feedback earlier, and iterate without starting from scratch. Unlike generic AI prototyping tools, Replica uses your team’s existing components, patterns, and documentation to guide what gets created. Designers define the guidance, while anyone on the team can use natural language in the GitHub Copilot app to create and refine prototypes that reflect how your product actually works. ### [What can you do with Replica?](#what-can-you-do-with-replica) * **Prototype with your design system:** Use your existing components, patterns, and documentation to guide AI-generated prototypes. * **Turn ideas into interactive experiences:** Describe what you want to explore in natural language, then see, test, and refine the result alongside your Copilot conversation. * **Collaborate and gather feedback:** Publish prototypes to an optional, self-hosted Replica Hub where teammates can explore them and leave comments. * **Adapt Replica to your team:** Customize the open-source tooling and guidance to fit your product and workflows. Replica helps teams move from conversations to tangible experiences faster, so they can test assumptions, explore possibilities, and make better-informed product decisions together. ### [Get started](#get-started) Replica is available now as an open-source project under the MIT license. You can start prototyping locally or set up Replica Hub to share prototypes with your team. Explore the repository for setup instructions, documentation, and examples. Explore [Replica on GitHub](https://github.com/github/replica). We’re excited to share what we’ve been building at GitHub Design and see what the community creates with it. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) ![GitHub developers pushed code 17.9 billion times in 2026 as AI agents reshape how software gets built](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fgithub-developers-pushed-code-179-billion-times-in-2026-as-ai-agents-reshape-how-software-gets-built-2_1793205452479.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #Dev # GitHub developers pushed code 17.9 billion times in 2026 as AI agents reshape how software gets built • ![Marta Kowalska](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Fmarta-kowalska.webp&w=64&q=75) [Marta Kowalska](/author/marta-kowalska) •11 min read Share this article GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report shows developer activity more than tripled in two years, with AI coding agents now starting over 40% of pull requests and developers spreading work across 47 different models. Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the 12 months ending September 30, 2026 — more than the previous two years combined. Commits across public and private repositories climbed to 34.3 billion, over three times the 2024 total. Merged pull requests topped 1.3 billion, averaging 3.5 million per day. The surge coincides with a fundamental shift in how developers work. AI coding agents moved from experimental tools to daily drivers. Repositories created this year with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as new repositories without one. By September, agents started more than 40% of pull requests, up from 17% in March. "The first move is now directing an agent, and review is how developers shape what comes back," said GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke in the report. ### Agents change the rhythm GitHub Actions ran a job 1,440 times every second this year — 124 million per day, more than three times 2025's volume. Developers merged over 30 million Dependabot pull requests to update dependencies, double last year's pace. Activity climbed steadily from January, then surged around June. That inflection point aligns with several industry shifts: more capable underlying models, better tooling around them, and agents that persist across days and orchestrate other specialized agents. Agents also began executing work in the cloud, not just on local machines. From June onward, about 55% of all commits came from brand-new repositories. But veteran developers stayed active. Contributors who pushed code in the past year have been on GitHub for an average of 36 months. Of those who opened a pull request in August, more than 75% pushed code again in September. The average developer now works across 10% more repositories than a year ago. Public contributions soared to 2.5 billion, more than double 2025's 1.12 billion. Maintainers like @kinlane contributed over 1 million times using agentic workflows to keep a machine-readable catalog of public API information current. @kim-em made more than 178,000 contributions maintaining mathlib, a community library of computer-checked mathematics. @andig, maintainer of the open-source EV charging controller evcc, contributed over 21,000 times. ### Developer population grows faster than projected GitHub now serves more than 225 million developers. The United States (38.3 million) and India (32 million) remain the largest communities, each adding over 10 million developers this year. Brazil added 3.28 million, the third-most of any country. Last year GitHub projected India would reach 57.5 million developers by 2030 and the United States 54.7 million. One year into that five-year window, every projected country has already closed at least a fifth of the distance to its 2030 figure. The United States has closed 38.6%; India 28.3%. Forecasting models now diverge sharply. GitHub ran more than 40 models projecting to 2031. About half predict "extreme" growth — more than tripling. Just under half predict "substantial" growth — doubling to tripling. Only three models show modest growth under 2x. The spread reflects how much the 2026 surge widened what seems plausible. Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # E2E Networks to add 5.4 MW NVIDIA Blackwell AI capacity E2E Networks plans to add 5.4 MW of NVIDIA Blackwell GPU capacity, increasing its total AI infrastructure to 14.6 MW. This expansion aims to meet rising demand for AI computing in India, supporting various AI workloads. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 28, 2026 at 07:45 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * E2E Networks will add 5.4 MW of NVIDIA Blackwell GPU capacity, reaching 14.6 MW total. * The expansion targets rising demand from Indian AI startups, enterprises, and public-sector organisations. * A ₹1,000 crore deal with an Indian sovereign AI company secures Blackwell GPUs until June 2029. * Revenue for Q3 2026 increased 411 per cent year-on-year to ₹223.76 crore. Indian cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure provider [E2E Networks](/tag/e2e+networks) will add 5.4 megawatts (MW) of computing capacity powered by [NVIDIA Blackwell](/tag/nvidia+blackwell) GPUs, the company said on Tuesday. This expansion will increase its total AI factory capacity to approximately 14.6 MW, a nearly 59 per cent rise. The proposed infrastructure will include NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and other Blackwell graphics processing units (GPUs). The additional capacity is intended to support AI workloads ranging from foundation model training to production inference and multimodal applications. E2E Networks reported growing demand from AI startups, model developers, research institutions, enterprises, and public-sector organisations. Organisations handling sensitive data are seeking computing infrastructure hosted in [India](/tag/india). Tarun Dua, founder and managing director of E2E Networks, noted that India’s AI builders are consuming AI tokens at previously un-heard scales in production. Dua added that the company is expanding capacity to allow organisations to keep their data within their own boundaries under national laws. This announcement follows previous investments and customer commitments. In August, E2E Networks signed a binding term sheet worth approximately ₹1,000 crore, excluding taxes. This agreement is with an unnamed Indian [sovereign AI](/tag/sovereign+ai) company for NVIDIA Blackwell cloud GPUs and related services through June 2029. The agreement converts deployed capacity from a pay-as-you-go model into a longer-term commitment. In September 2025, the company also received an order worth approximately ₹177 crore under the [IndiaAI Mission](/tag/indiaai+mission). This order is to provide GPU computing resources to AI company Gnani AI for 360 days, including NVIDIA H100 and H200 GPUs. For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, E2E Networks reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹223.76 crore. This was up about 411 per cent year-on-year, with a net profit of ₹72.70 crore compared to a loss in the prior year. The company attributed this growth partly to contributions from Blackwell GPUs and improved utilisation. Founded in 2009, E2E Networks provides [cloud computing](/tag/cloud+computing) and GPU infrastructure for AI and machine-learning workloads. It is listed on the National Stock Exchange and the BSE. In November 2024, [Larsen & Toubro](/tag/larsen+%26+toubro) announced a strategic partnership with E2E Networks, planning to acquire a 21 per cent equity stake. This partnership combines E2E’s cloud platform with L&T’s data centre and cloud services capabilities. E2E Networks did not disclose the investment amount or commissioning timeline for the latest 5.4 MW expansion. ## Comments ![Comment...

Infra & Chips.content: # Oracle Expands Nvidia AI Chip Deal, Adds Google, Cerebras and SambaNova as Capex Targets $95 Billion Rajani Baburajan Oracle is expanding its artificial intelligence infrastructure partnership with Nvidia to multi-gigawatt scale while adding AI processors from Google, Cerebras Systems and SambaNova Systems to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The strategy aims to strengthen Oracle’s position in the global AI cloud market by offering customers more choices for AI model training, inference and enterprise AI applications. Oracle’s AI Chip Strategy The announcement, made on October 27, 2026, represents a significant expansion of Oracle’s AI infrastructure strategy as technology companies accelerate investments in data centers, AI processors and cloud computing. Oracle is also targeting capital expenditure of $90 billion to $95 billion in fiscal 2027, highlighting the substantial investment required to support demand for AI computing capacity. The company has not disclosed the financial value of its expanded Nvidia agreement or the planned purchases from other AI chip suppliers. Oracle and Nvidia Expand AI Infrastructure to Multi-Gigawatt Scale Oracle and Nvidia are expanding their partnership to deploy Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin AI computing systems across OCI Superclusters. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has previously indicated that Vera Rubin systems could generate $40 billion in Nvidia revenue for every gigawatt of deployment. Oracle and Nvidia have also announced the general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs on OCI. Each NVL72 rack connects 72 GPUs through Nvidia’s NVLink technology, while Oracle’s networking architecture supports infrastructure scaling across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. Oracle plans to introduce [Nvidia HGX Rubin NVL8 systems](https://www.oracle.com/news/announcement/ai-world-nvidia-and-oracle-expand-nvidia-vera-rubin-to-multi-gigawatt-scale-2026-10-27/) featuring eight Rubin GPUs, two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 processors, 4 TB of DDR5 memory and 6.4 Tbps networking. The smaller configuration will give enterprises an alternative to large rack-scale deployments for AI training, fine-tuning and inference. Oracle Adds Google TPU Chips to Challenge Nvidia’s Dominance Oracle is diversifying its AI infrastructure by introducing Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) developed by Google. The agreement will make Oracle Cloud Infrastructure the first hyperscale cloud platform outside Google Cloud to offer Google’s TPU technology. Google’s eighth-generation TPU portfolio includes processors optimized for different AI workloads. The TPU 8t architecture targets large-scale AI model training, while TPU 8i focuses on inference workloads, including applications involving multiple AI agents. Oracle expects Google’s TPU offerings to become available on OCI in 2027. The partnership will allow customers to select between Nvidia GPUs and Google TPUs according to their AI computing requirements. For enterprise customers, the availability of alternative processors could improve infrastructure flexibility and create opportunities to optimize AI computing costs. The arrangement could also help organizations run AI applications closer to their existing Oracle databases, reducing the need to transfer enterprise data between cloud environments. However, actual cost savings will depend on processor pricing, application compatibility, utilization and workload performance. Cerebras Partnership Targets High-Speed AI Inference Oracle is also partnering with Cerebras Systems to introduce high-speed AI inference services on OCI. Cerebras specializes in wafer-scale computing technology designed to accelerate AI model execution. Its Wafer-Scale Engine integrates computing and memory resources on a single large processor, reducing the movement of data between separate chips. [Oracle Cloud](/tag/oracle+cloud) Infrastructure ([OCI](/tag/oci)) plans to deploy Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and AI inference chips from [OpenAI](/tag/openai), [Cerebras](/tag/cerebras), [SambaNova](/tag/sambanova), and [Positron AI](/tag/positron+ai). The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine for high-speed AI inference is slated for deployment in 2027. Oracle also plans to deploy OpenAI’s Jalapeño inference accelerators, developed with Broadcom, though no specific OCI availability date was provided. SambaNova is collaborating with Oracle to deploy its SN50 inference chips in OCI, with no availability date specified. Industry analysts noted that Oracle's adoption of these additional AI accelerators provides customers with greater flexibility.
