Infra & Chips.content: # citybiz+ Simplismart Raises $14M to Expand AI Inference Infrastructure ### San Francisco-based Simplismart raised $14 million in Series B funding led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The company develops software that helps enterprises optimize AI inference costs, latency, and GPU utilization across cloud and on-premises infrastructure. Customers include HeyGen, Higgsfield and Shiprocket. Simplismart reported 14-fold growth in annualized revenue run rate over six months, as it expands its platform and international cloud partnerships. ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Simplismart.png) San Francisco-based [**Simplismart**](https://simplismart.ai/) has **raised $14 million in a Series B round led by Dallas Venture Capital,** with participation from **Nvidia, Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax** as the AI inference infrastructure company seeks to reduce the cost of running artificial intelligence models in production, shifting attention from model development toward the computing infrastructure required to deliver AI applications reliably at scale. Simplismart develops software that sits between AI models and graphics processing units (GPUs), handling model deployment, performance optimization and ongoing operations. Its inference engine evaluates configurations against requirements such as latency, throughput and cost, while its orchestration platform manages workloads across cloud providers, geographic regions and on-premises infrastructure. “The industry has spent years pushing the limits of what AI models can do. With frontier-class open models now readily available, access alone is no longer enough to set a business apart. The advantage comes from how you run them: what each interaction costs, how quickly the application responds, and whether it stays reliable as demand grows,” said **[Amritanshu Jain](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jainamritanshu/),** co-founder and CEO of Simplismart. Jain is an Indian technology entrepreneur. He earned a Bachelor of Engineering degree from Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS), Pilani. Before launching Simplismart, Jain worked as a machine learning engineer at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, developing cloud and machine learning systems, and at Capillary Technologies, where he contributed to machine learning applications and production-scale data infrastructure. As companies adopt open-weight models and build applications around generative AI, operating costs can become a significant constraint. Simplismart said its software is designed to help enterprises and cloud providers manage GPU resources, balance response times against operating costs, and scale deployments without independently configuring every environment. The company serves customers in video generation, voice, multimodal applications and enterprise software, including HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema. Simplismart also helps cloud infrastructure companies seeking to monetize computing capacity without building their own inference software. Its model differs from businesses that purchase or reserve GPU capacity for resale because it provides the software layer that lets third-party cloud operators offer managed AI services under their own brands. Dallas Venture Capital (DVC) is a venture capital firm with offices in Dallas and Hyderabad that invests in software-as-a-service, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, data, DevOps, and artificial intelligence. Since 2021, DVC has operated its second fund alongside the DVC India Fund. Infra & Chips.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # OpenAI Pursues Direct Purchase of Google TPUs, Testing NVIDIA's Dominance [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) OpenAI is reportedly pursuing a plan to buy Google's in-house AI accelerator, the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), directly. OpenAI, which has until now rented TPUs, is expanding its cooperation with Google to outright chip purchases—a move that could introduce an alternative to an AI computing market centered on NVIDIA GPUs. Google is also widening external sales by supplying TPUs through Oracle Cloud. Still, OpenAI maintains close ties with NVIDIA, including up to $105 billion in credit support for an Ohio data center. The market is watching Alphabet's third-quarter results, due Oct. 28, for cloud growth and progress in the TPU business. ##### Key Elements OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, is reportedly pursuing a plan to directly purchase Google's in-house artificial intelligence (AI) accelerator, the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). OpenAI, which has until now rented Google TPUs, is broadening the scope of its cooperation to buying the chips outright. The move is seen as one that could crack the landscape of AI computing infrastructure, which is concentrated on NVIDIA GPUs. Infra & Chips.content: ![]() ![GuruFocus](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/gurufocus--theme-light.svg) ![GuruFocus](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/gurufocus--theme-dark.svg) # Nvidia Faces Fresh Challenge as OpenAI Expands AI Bets ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/nvidia.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/openai.svg) OpenAI is reportedly planning to buy artificial intelligence chips from Alphabet's (GOOG) Google, a potentially significant shift as the ChatGPT maker looks to diversify the enormous amount of computing infrastructure needed to train and deploy its models. Final terms of any potential agreement have not yet been determined, according to multiple media reports. OpenAI is already one of the world's largest buyers of Nvidia [![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/nvidia.svg)NVDA](/symbols/NASDAQ-NVDA/) GPUs, which remain central to both AI model training and inference. ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/nvidia.svg) A deal with Google would therefore be notable because it could give OpenAI another major source of AI computing capacity while reducing its reliance on a single chip supplier. For Google, the implications could be equally important. The company has spent years developing its own AI accelerators to support internal workloads. Selling more of those chips to outside AI developers could turn that investment into a much larger commercial business. The reported talks also highlight how rapidly the AI infrastructure market is evolving. Leading AI companies increasingly need massive quantities of specialized processors, power and data-center capacity, making supply diversification strategically important. That does not necessarily mean Nvidia is being displaced. OpenAI's compute requirements are large enough that the company could continue purchasing substantial quantities of Nvidia GPUs even while adding Google chips to its infrastructure. Instead, the move would suggest that AI developers increasingly want access to multiple hardware platforms rather than depending on one architecture. **Investor Takeaway** I think the biggest potential read-through is for **Google's AI infrastructure ambitions**. If OpenAI becomes a meaningful buyer of Google-designed chips, Alphabet would not simply be competing with OpenAI at the model level. It would also be supplying infrastructure to one of its biggest AI rivals. For Nvidia, the development is worth watching but does not automatically imply lost demand. OpenAI's compute needs continue to expand, and adding another supplier could simply reflect how difficult it is to secure enough capacity. For investors, the key things to watch are **the size of any agreement, which Google chips OpenAI ultimately adopts, deployment timing and whether other major AI developers follow with similar multi-supplier strategies**. The AI chip race may be becoming less about choosing one winner. The deal was announced during a visit to Astana by NVIDIA Founder and Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang. Under the agreement, Firebird is expanding beyond its first AI factory in Armenia into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a US export licence for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase, being built with Kazakhtelecom at Data Centre Valley, is targeting a commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027. A planned second phase would take Firebird's potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to about 500 megawatts. It also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local startups, research and talent development through funding, access to computing resources and research partnerships. Kazakhtelecom, the country's largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty. It also plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in Data Centre Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region. **Broader push** The infrastructure build-out comes as Kazakhstan pushes to develop domestic AI models and applications. During a public discussion at the Alem.AI centre in Astana, Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev said the country wants AI systems that reflect its language and culture. "We want AI that understands and speaks Kazakh and captures cultural contexts and cultural specifics," Madiyev said. Huang said local data would be central to that effort and argued that Kazakhstan could use its energy resources to support AI production. "Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence," Huang said. He also stressed the importance of retaining control over national datasets. "Your country's data is your natural resource. It belongs to you," Huang said. The discussion also covered the use of AI in mining, mineral processing, agriculture, transport and logistics. Madiyev raised the prospect of Kazakhstan becoming a hub for training models for robots and other physical systems, an idea Huang welcomed. "If you have ambition, and I believe you do, AI will lift your nation," Huang said. "AI will lift your people." **Startup activity** The Astana event also brought news that NVIDIA is investing in Higgsfield AI, a startup founded in Kazakhstan. Huang praised the company's founders during the public session. "The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies," Huang said. Under the agreement, Firebird is expanding beyond its first AI factory in Armenia into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a US export licence for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase, being built with Kazakhtelecom at Data Centre Valley, is targeting a commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027. A planned second phase would take Firebird's potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to about 500 megawatts. It also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local startups, research and talent development through funding, access to computing resources and research partnerships. Kazakhtelecom, the country's largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty. It also plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in Data Centre Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region. **Broader push** The infrastructure build-out comes as Kazakhstan pushes to develop domestic AI models and applications. During a public discussion at the Alem.AI centre in Astana, Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev said the country wants AI systems that reflect its language and culture. "We want AI that understands and speaks Kazakh and captures cultural contexts and cultural specifics," Madiyev said. Huang said local data would be central to that effort and argued that Kazakhstan could use its energy resources to support AI production. "Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence," Huang said. He also stressed the importance of retaining control over national datasets. "Your country's data is your natural resource. It belongs to you," Huang said. The discussion also covered the use of AI in mining, mineral processing, agriculture, transport and logistics. Madiyev raised the prospect of Kazakhstan becoming a hub for training models for robots and other physical systems, an idea Huang welcomed. "If you have ambition, and I believe you do, AI will lift your nation," Huang said. "AI will lift your people." **Startup activity** The Astana event also brought news that NVIDIA is investing in Higgsfield AI, a startup founded in Kazakhstan. Huang praised the company's founders during the public session. "The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies," Huang said. Higgsfield is expanding its AI infrastructure with NVIDIA Vera Rubin through cloud service providers as demand grows for its generative media products.
